variant: Rutan Model 74 Defiant, the plans-built homebuilt (Fred Keller prototype, 1983; plans 1984-85), 2x Lycoming O-320 160 hp, fixed-pitch wood props. Where noted, values are for the Model 40 proof-of-concept prototype N78RA (1978), which has a shorter wing and canard span.
config: push-pull twin canard (centerline thrust), swept aft wing with winglets

span.note: RAF Model 74 plans brochure spec table, CP38 (Oct 1983). Model 40 prototype N78RA: 29 ft 2 in (CP17 Jul 1978 comparison table). Other published values (secondary, unsourced): 30 ft 9 in (Wikipedia), 31 ft 5 in (Skymaster site/Jane's), 29 ft 7 in (Plane & Pilot)

area.note: Model 74 per CP38; Model 40 prototype 127.3 sq ft (CP17). Wikipedia's 139.4 sq ft is unsourced; whether it includes the canard is unknown

sweep_le_deg.note: E: inference. CP22 (Oct 1979) says the Long-EZ's new wing has a '23-degree L.E. sweep, Eppler airfoil, and wing attachments ... similar to the Defiant'. Defiant figure not published

wing.airfoil: Eppler section (exact designation not published; RAF says the Long-EZ wing airfoil is 'similar to that on the Defiant', CP21/CP22). The Long-EZ wing is commonly given as a modified Eppler 1230, so that is our inference only
wing.winglets: yes; winglets with rudders give directional stability, canted inboard about 3 in from vertical (CP17 Q&A). Model 74 had revised winglets. Heights and areas not found. A separate small ventral rudder sits forward under the nose, offset to port (Wikipedia, Hiller Museum, CP38: 'rudder is only one foot from the pilot's rudder pedals')

canard_or_htail.airfoil: not published. CP34 (Oct 1982): the Defiant canard runs at about twice the Long-EZ's Reynolds number (~1 million); it has a very mild nose-up change in rain and no measurable takeoff-speed effect. Elevators act as a full-span slotted flap (CP38)
canard_or_htail.note: Model 74 canard span is larger than N78RA's (CP38, CP54). T&T 2026: a folding-canard mod on N171D cuts span by 'about six feet' so the aircraft fits T-hangars, which implies a canard span well over 6 ft (unquantified). Canard static-test issue: CP52 (Jul 1987) refers to 'the CP51 announcement of Don Foreman's Defiant canard failure in a static load test conducted for the British CAA'. In a follow-up Florida test of a repaired spare canard, a lift tab failed at 5 g, which RAF attributed to an unrepresentative jig (CP52). We did not confirm what fix, if any, followed.

vtail.note: Directional stability from two wingtip winglets with rudders; plus a small ventral rudder forward under the nose for control (designed to 'have no effect on stability', CP38). Yaw damping 1-2 cycles (CP38).

length.note: Wikipedia infobox, uncited; treat as unverified (E: secondary)

cabin_width.note: elbow width front; 43 in at rear seats (CP38)

fuselage.note: Overall height 9.33 ft (Wikipedia, uncited). Cabin: CP17 says '2 inches wider elbow room, 8 inches longer cabin' than a Beech Duchess. Side-hinged canopy. Semi-supine seats. Model 74 has more rear headroom than N78RA.

nacelles_or_booms: No nacelles. Both engines are on the fuselage centerline: one tractor in the nose, one pusher at the tail behind the cabin. Wing-root/rear-engine cowling fairs into the wing root. Ken Brock 8 in prop extension recommended for faired cowls (CP43). Cowl dimensions not found.
gear: fixed main gear in fairings (wheel pants); nose gear retracts (Mooney-derived nose gear assembly, CP43). No flaps. Vlo 130 KIAS / Vle 150 (T&T 2026)
cooling: Air-cooled. Both engines use updraft cooling designed for strong positive pressure gain with power and AoA. No cowl flaps and no oil coolers on the prototype; CHT 370 F in cruise, oil 190-200 F in hot-day climb (CP17, Rutan). Rear engine: on at least one later build (T&T 2026, N171D context) the original P-51-style belly scoop overheated and over-revved, and was replaced with two 'armpit' scoops ramming air into each cylinder bank. Scale of the problem across the fleet unknown.

diameter.note: fixed-pitch, Model 40 prototype (CP17 comparison table). Props were Kevlar/wood (CP17). Front and rear pitched differently (Skymaster article). N78RA later had Hoffmann constant-speed feathering props (CP47-CP49); Rutan withheld approval of any CS installation (CP49)

engine.model: 2x Lycoming O-320 (150/160 hp); plans allowed 150, 160 or 180 hp (O-360) per engine (CP38)

mtow.note: Model 74 gross weight; Model 40 prototype 2900 lb (CP17)

empty.note: basic empty; equipped empty 1680 lb (CP38). Prototype IFR empty 1585 lb (CP17)

max_landing.note: pilot-report spec block: max landing = gross

fuel_usable.note: spec table: 115 gal (text: one 58-gal tank per engine, crossfeed available). Prototype N78RA normal load 90.5 gal (CP19); T&T N171D 108 gal

fleet_size_for_rate.note: T&T 2026: 'only about 30 Defiant airframes are believed to have been completed, and roughly 20 remain active'. Wikipedia: 19 FAA-registered in 2005; 176 plans sets sold (Linehan 2011); T&T says 'nearly 200'

safety.pattern: RECORD: The record is small and has no engine-failure or asymmetric-thrust (Vmc-type) accident. The largest group is the retractable nose gear: landings with the nose gear not down or not locked (SEA06CA097, where maintenance records showed two earlier repeats in 18 years; WPR10LA219, where the down-and-locked marks are hard to see by the pilot's ankle), a nose gear collapse (ERA17LA054), and a German gear-up landing in 2013. Fatal 1 (CHI05LA257): an aborted takeoff overran a 2160 ft turf strip. The NTSB quotes the owner's manual: the Defiant is 'a heavy wing-loading aircraft that required longer runways than typical general-aviation twin engine airplanes'. Fatal 2 (ERA18FA189): erratic steep descending turn after a go-around, cause undetermined, no engine anomaly. Other: canopy opened in flight after a builder-modified latch (CHI97LA234); runway excursion (Germany 2013). Designer record: CP53 (Oct 1987) reports NG-2 nose-gear retract-link failures on three Defiants (Gray, Best, Cardinale). Cardinale's aircraft ran off the runway. RAF sent all plans owners a mandatory nose-gear change dated 15 Sep 1987 and warned that a collapse could grind through the lower cowl into the carburetor bowl and cause a fire ('Ground your Defiant until you have completed this change'). Design documents: Rutan (CP49) refused to approve constant-speed props. With centerline thrust the pilot gets no yaw cue to tell which engine failed, an unfeathered CS prop leaves inadequate single-engine climb, and the aft prop's blades/hub see vibratory bending in the wake (fatigue risk). CP47 warns the accident rate may be 'considerably higher' on CS/feathering conversions. Some builders did install CS props (CP47: first Defiant flown with CS props). N78RA's front engine had a fuel-line blockage from build debris that showed only on the fuel-pressure gauge (CP54). INFERENCE: The configuration did what it promised on engine-out control. Its residual risks are the retract nose gear (a 'gear-up' trap on an otherwise fixed-gear aircraft), long takeoff runs from 22 psf wing loading with fixed-pitch props and no flaps, and canard pitch sensitivity. Rear-engine cooling problems and rear-prop fatigue are design points to engineer out, not causes in the accident record.

why_died_detail: Rutan positioned N78RA as 'merely a proof-of-concept prototype for aerodynamic research' with 'no plans to market' (CP17, 1978). RAF announced a type-certified 5-seat derivative in 1979 (CP20), but certification financing never came (Wikipedia; Skymaster article: certification cost 'scared off all the prospective investors'). The homebuilt Model 74 plans came out in 1984. On 13 July 1985 RAF stopped marketing all homebuilt plans to cut overhead in a 'declining market place' and kept only builder support (CP45). That ended Defiant plans sales after roughly 176-200 sets. The engine installation plans were still unfinished in Jan 1986 (CP47), and Brock made only 50 sets of prefab metal parts (CP47). The aircraft is a big build ('two Long-EZs', 2000+ hr per RAF; one builder reports 7500-8000 hr, T&T). Only about 30 were completed. The record does not point to a safety-driven demise: the type died of business choices and build burden. A revival would need complete engine-installation documentation, modern prefab parts, a robust nose-gear indication/lock or fixed nose gear, and possibly a folding canard for hangarage (one builder's mod, T&T).
rights_hints: Designed by Burt Rutan at Rutan Aircraft Factory (RAF). RAF stopped selling plans on 13 July 1985 but committed to continued builder support (CP45). Plane & Pilot (2010): '(No plans available.)'. RAF published the Canard Pusher newsletter into the 2000s (archive through CP109, 2002, at http://www.cozybuilders.org/Canard_Pusher/). We found nothing on who holds the Defiant plans copyright today or whether Rutan would license it. The prototype N78RA belongs to the Hiller Aviation Museum (https://www.hiller.org/defiant-40/). Rutan insisted #40 was 'just a proof-of-concept aircraft and not a prototype' (T&T 2026).
